 A proper food safety culture aligns your restaurant’s daily food safety protocols and your emergency response protocols. Both are necessary to protect your guests, trading partners, and brand. By Roger Hancock, CEO of Recall InfoLink - 
11.13.2026 
 Restaurants spend substantial time, money, and resources to build and maintain a strong food safety culture. This is especially critical after recent widespread recalls, including lettuce that was distributed to numerous restaurant locations this summer, setting records for the largest Cyclospora contamination event to date. This one incident had a massive footprint, providing a real-world example of why recall readiness must be part of restaurants’ food safety cultures.
 Recall readiness is food safety culture tested under pressure. It’s more than displaying a safety certificate on the wall or passing independent audits. A proper food safety culture aligns your restaurant’s daily food safety protocols and your emergency response protocols . Both are necessary to protect your guests, trading partners, and brand.
 Despite advances, innovations, and prevention strategies, some food safety breaches remain inevitable. A supplier could unknowingly ship contaminated lettuce to a national restaurant chain involving them in one of the year’s largest recalls, as we saw this summer. Your restaurant brand isn’t immune to a large-scale crisis, even if your employees follow exceptional food safety practices. That means, as part of your food safety culture efforts, you must ensure that everyone, from the corporate office down to your points of sale, is recall ready .
 What does recall readiness look like inside a restaurant operation?
 Practical technology workflows. Tech tools improve visibility, traceability, and communication, making it exponentially faster to identify, contain, and remove contaminated products. All trading partners must have usable traceability records and other product distribution data that automates tracking workflows. This enables trading partners to accurately and quickly confirm where affected products went and whether they have been removed from the chain, including restaurant kitchens.
 Connected tech systems. When trading partners use interoperable systems, it enables faster action, more targeted efforts, and more complete recall resolution. Rely on a connected system built on standardized data that’s easy to pull and share. Since tech tools, data standards, and resources have improved dramatically in recent years, it’s now easier, faster, and more accurate to pinpoint exactly where a product came from, where it traveled, and whether it was part of a recall—but only if you’re able to do so in collaboration with the rest of your supply chain.
 Data management. As both supply chain complexity and average recall scope are on the rise, data management is more important than ever before. Prioritize transparency and documentation, ensuring that you have current contact data, traceability records, and the ability to confirm that key actions—like product removal—have occurred. Effective data management requires systems to be implemented and aligned before a recall occurs. FSMA 204 enforcement has been delayed to July 2028 , but companies can’t afford to wait. Since data systems take time to implement, restaurants must act now.
 Advanced planning. Restaurant companies must prepare in advance, with a written recall plan, assigned roles and responsibilities, and proper tech frameworks in place. Implement ongoing training to ensure that everyone knows what to do during a recall. Since recalls are supply chain events , not single company events , work collaboratively with your training partners to prepare. Mock recall simulations with your trading partners and operators must be a core component of these collaborative efforts. Importantly, companies that do the best jobs managing a recall are the ones that did the work in advance.
 A cross-functional team. Assemble a cross-functional team that includes quality, operations, PR, IT, and legal representatives. Ensure that everyone is working from the same playbook and following the same process. Since roles and responsibilities were defined in advance, the team should be able to galvanize and act quickly during a recall.
 Employee empowerment. Empower employees to be actively involved in the food safety and recall culture. Reiterate your commitment to no-blame reporting , where frontline staff can freely report safety or recall process concerns without fear of repercussions. When every employee serves as a food safety ambassador—with everyone responsible for identifying potential concerns—it helps protect the food, company, partners, and guests.
 Supply chain familiarity. There’s no doubt that the supply chain has become more complicated, as supplier consolidation, cross-border sourcing, and distribution complexity contribute to today’s larger recall scope. Evolving supply chain dynamics—including fewer, larger suppliers serving a wider network of retailers, and international chains—mean that one point of failure can quickly become a widespread, multi-state crisis. Since a single contamination event (like contaminated lettuce or jalapeños ) can impact multiple restaurant brands and locations, familiarity with your sources of supply helps you determine unequivocally whether your specific kitchen is at risk.
 Strong communication. Communication is a critical component of a recall. Be prepared to communicate clearly, quickly, and accurately to inform key audiences—including employees, partners, and guests—about what happened and what happens next. Pushing out real-time information, including updates as they become available, helps protect public health, reassure nervous guests, and preserve your brand’s reputation.
 Top-down commitment to recall readiness. Food safety culture and recall readiness starts at the top. Brand leadership must prioritize food safety culture and recall preparedness, explaining why this matters. Emphasizing the rationale for these efforts, rather just telling staff what to do, helps secure buy-in and participation across the organization.
 Food safety culture isn’t truly effective without recall readiness because a culture focused solely on prevention will likely fail during a crisis. Recall readiness tests the strength of your company’s food safety culture when something does go wrong. Once a recall is initiated, the company must instantly shift from daily food safety protocols into an organized, coordinated, unflappable crisis response. Recall readiness ensures that internal and external teams are prepared for this, knowing exactly what to do and how to do it.
 Roger Hancock, CEO of Recall InfoLink , is one of the world’s foremost experts on recalls, with experience that spans the retail, tech, data, regulatory and supply chain. Recall InfoLink makes recalls faster, easier, and more accurate across the supply chain to protect consumers and brands. As the only company focused entirely on recalls, Recall InfoLink’s solutions drive immediate action, streamline the recall process, and simplify compliance. Roger is also a steering committee member of the Alliance for Recall Ready Communities .
